To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have cloned and characterized a number of T. taenia eformis antigens, but that we have yet to identify the antigen(s) that will protect against infection.

(1) we have identified 7 antigen families expressed by T. taeniaesiformis; (2) we have developed methods for identifying and purifying the native antigens; (3) we have shown that the antigens do not protect against subsequent infection in mice.
the antigenic complexity of Taenia taemiaeformis has been greatly underestimated and that no protective antigens have been identified.

the identification and characterization of antigens of T. taeniaefornis, with particular emphasis on the isolation of those antigens which are likely to be involved in host protective immunity and which may be useful as diagnostic antigens.
the isolation, characterization, and immunogenic properties of Taenia taeniiformis antigens expressed as fusion proteins in Escherichiacoli.
the isolation and identification of T. taeniaesformis antigens and their expression in E. coli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the antigens identified to date have no role in host protective immunity, but this does not rule out their potential usefulness as diagnostic antigens.
we have identified a number of antigen genes from T. taeniaesformis which are expressed in E. coli as fusion proteins.
the antigens described in this paper have not been shown to be protective against infection, but that this does not preclude the possibility that they may be so.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been able to identify a number of T. taenia eformis antigens and have developed a number of techniques for the rapid immunological characterization of cloned genes.

, despite the availability of a large collection of T. taenia eformis antigens, we have not been able to isolate a single molecule which is a good candidate for use as a vaccine against infection with this parasite.
, despite the large number of antigene-expressing clones isolated, we have been unable to identify any of the candidate host-protecting antigens.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immunological analysis of cloned parasite antigens is not a trivial task.
the use of a polyclonal antiserum to screen for antigen-expressing cDNA clones can be a useful approach to identifying parasite genes that encode antigens of potential use in vaccine development.
the use of a polyspecific antiserum to screen a cDNA library is a powerful technique, but that the identification of the corresponding native T. taeniensis molecules is not trivial.
